report:
**Conclusion: No — ivermectin does not lower the risk of death in COVID-19.**

The best available evidence from large randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and recent meta-analyses shows no mortality benefit from ivermectin in COVID-19 patients.

**Key evidence:**

- A **2024 meta-analysis of 33 RCTs (n = 10,489)** found that ivermectin "did not have an effect in reducing the risk of mortality in patients with COVID-19" ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405844024036788)).

- The **ACTIV-6 trial**, a large randomized controlled trial published in October 2022, found ivermectin was not effective as a COVID-19 treatment ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivermectin_during_the_COVID-19_pandemic)).

- The **TOGETHER trial** (NEJM, 2022), the largest randomized double-blind trial at the time, found ivermectin did not reduce hospitalization or prolonged ED observation among outpatients ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2115869)).

- In **November 2023, the WHO updated its guidelines** to strongly recommend against ivermectin for COVID-19 treatment, citing a lack of evidence and biological plausibility ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivermectin_during_the_COVID-19_pandemic); [WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/feature-stories/detail/who-advises-that-ivermectin-only-be-used-to-treat-covid-19-within-clinical-trials)).

Early smaller studies and observational data suggested possible benefit, but these were methodologically weak and their findings were not replicated in large, well-conducted RCTs. The current scientific consensus, supported by the WHO, FDA, and Infectious Diseases Society of America, is that ivermectin should not be used to treat COVID-19 outside of clinical trials.
